From the experimental data at 1150 h (represented by ‘A’ in the equation below), the corrosion rate per year was obtained based on linear extrapolation as follows: 𝐴×8760 CR [microns/year] = (1b) 1150 Figure 11 compares corrosion rates in microns per year for the tested samples based on both direct metal loss thickness measurements after 1150 h of exposure (Eq. 1b: orange bars) and from parabolic rate fitting (Eq. 1a) extrapolated to a system lifetime of 20 years (blue bars). The metal loss thickness based on linear extrapolation provides a conservative estimate, as it implies a higher corrosion rate than the parabolic fit. The observed corrosion rates are consistent with the McConomy curves [25], which predict average rates of 10–15 microns/year for austenitic 18Cr-8/10Ni steels. Corten B showed the highest rate of corrosion. Overall, the results from corrosion tests demonstrate that austenitic stainless steel 300 series alloys are highly compatible with sulfur under the conditions expected for our thermal storage technology. Specifically, SS-304 and SS-316 samples subjected to > 1000 hours of isothermal exposure in molten sulfur at 300oC exhibited corrosion rates below 35 microns per year based on the conservative linear kinetics, thereby confirming their suitability for long-term operation. Figure 11: Summary of the corrosion rate obtained from the parabolic rate law (see Fig. 20) and experimental data measurement of metal loss after 1150h of immersion in molten sulfur cycling between 150 oC and 300 oC Intertek also subjected the samples before and after exposure to tensile strength and yield strength testing, cross-section analysis to verify that the corrosion layer did not affect the underlying non-corroded metal or adversely affect mechanical strength. Mechanical testing provides a good proxy for evaluating whether sulfidation products compromised grain boundaries and structural integrity. Figure 12 summarizes tensile and yield strength of the coupons before and after exposure. Except for aluminum, all alloys showed an increase in strength, likely due to age hardening. Aluminum, on the other hand, has a low Page 30 of 87 DE-EE0009329 Element 16 Technologies, Inc. melting point in comparison to steel and stainless steel. Aluminum, which has a lower melting point than steel and stainless steel, exhibited strength loss after exposure to high- temperature sulfur. As noted earlier, Aluminum was mainly investigated for possible use as heat transfer performance enhancement feature (e.g. fins) due to its high sulfidation resistance. No reduction in strength was observed for carbon steel or stainless-steel alloys.
